content_en:
Mark Zuckerberg is barrelling toward a future in which an autonomous network of AI agents will run our lives — shopping for us, working for us, talking to other people’s AI agents for us. Are humans ready for this very specific and unrelenting vision of a life in which we communicate primarily through bot proxies? Actually, don’t answer that. The more urgent question coming off Meta’s quarterly earnings call Wednesday night is more likely to be: “Is he?”

# In Meta’s version of the future, I’ll have my Muse call your Muse

“... everyone is just going to have to adapt,” Meta’s chief financial officer Susan Li said during the third-quarter earnings call.

Zuckerberg is staking Meta’s future on Muse, the personal AI agent it released to the general public last month. It’s early days, but Zuckerberg told investors on Wednesday’s call that he sees a future where “billions” of people are using Muse, and those people’s Muses are talking to and transacting with other people’s Muses in a “large-scale Muse network.”

The Muses will be “extremely capable” personal agents that will help us achieve our goals and improve our lives in “whatever ways you want,” Zuckerberg said, “whether that’s improving your relationships, helping you save time, save money, build a business, create new things, or anything else that you can dream of.” By this logic, Zuckerberg says, we’ll all be so hooked on Muse that it will eventually generate more revenue per user for Meta than Instagram and Facebook, which as of today, bring in pretty much all of the money Meta makes.

This ecosystem of personal AI agents “can work with your friends and your families, and if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” Zuckerberg said. “I think that getting that all to work well together is going to unlock tremendous value at scale.”

Zuckerberg predicts that Muse will be “highly profitable” in just a few years.

All of this should sound great — if not a little freaky — to investors, who probably tuned into Meta’s call hoping Zuckerberg would have some justification for the hundreds of billions of dollars his company is currently spending on AI data centers. But, if anyone was hoping for more than a concept of a plan, they didn’t get one.

To be fair to Muse, Zuckerberg shared a few promising data points. To date, the app has been downloaded and set up by more than 10 million users in the US and Canada, making it one of Meta’s “most successful launches ever,” according to Zuckerberg. He did not share specific retention numbers, but said that a quarter of people who downloaded Muse initially are using it daily. He sees the biggest opportunity in commerce. A quarter of Muse users are shopping through the platform, Zuckerberg said, and are spending on average more than $200 per purchase.

Meta earns a fee for every commercial transaction that takes place on Muse. Zuckerberg’s thinking seems to be that if AI agents are doing the shopping, the potential number of transactions that could take place on the platform is, essentially, unlimited. Unlike the average consumer, AI agents don’t sleep. In theory, they’re available 24/7 to scrape the Internet, generate product recommendations, and buy things, constantly, in real time.

Meta didn’t offer any details as to how all of this will actually work in practice, which makes sense given the very legitimate concerns about how the company handles data privacy. In September, a YouTuber said his Muse agent sent a stranger to his home in the middle of the night while arranging a Facebook Marketplace transaction on his behalf. When Muse launched last month, Zuckerberg claimed it was “built for privacy and security from the ground up,” but there have been reports of agents leaking content from users’ private conversations. A Canadian bank executive told *Bloomberg* earlier this week that it would consider blocking Muse from accessing its customers’ financial data.

Zuckerberg seems to think if people get on board with Muse, enterprise will have to follow. But, what if people don’t want to? What if they can’t afford to? Someone has to pay for all the stuff the bots are buying in this fever dream of a never-ending, *Supermarket Sweep* episode taking place inside our phones — or Muse Charms, if you’d rather. New research from the University of Michigan shows that consumer sentiment in the US is at an all-time low as gas prices and inflation continue to creep up.

If Meta knows that all of this sounds dystopian and a little bizarre, it does not care.

“Agents are going to be an important part of how reality evolves, and everyone is just going to have to adapt,” Meta’s chief financial officer Susan Li said when one investor on the call asked about potential “friction points” in getting businesses on board with the Muse plan. After all, Meta says Muse will likely remain free for consumers, while businesses will be expected to cover the transaction fees.

Meta really does need Muse to work. The company’s capex is through the roof, and other financial obligations are piling up. It plans to spend between $135 billion and $145 billion in 2026, double what it spent last year. As of yesterday, it owes New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found it had violated the state’s consumer protection laws. Meta, and the rest of Big Tech for that matter, is under increasing pressure to show that its AI investments will be worth it.

Forget consumers — it’s not clear if Meta itself can afford its plans. Zuckerberg stated clearly on the call that the reason it hasn’t launched Muse internationally is because of compute efficiency.

It’s incredibly expensive and energy-intensive to run GPUs at the level that a network of Muses would require, and Meta seems to have reached the limit of what it can achieve with its current data center operations. Zuckerberg told investors the plan is to “10x” the cost-efficiency of its compute next year. He didn’t explain how the company plans to do this. Luckily for him — and possibly the rest of us — there is already research on how data centers can maximize compute capacity with energy use strategies that also reduce strain on the electric grid. Maybe he’ll read it.

Ultimately, Muse won’t be profitable and won’t succeed if Meta can’t figure out how to get its compute costs down. Zuckerberg said it himself.

“One of the biggest constraints so far is that because this is a compute-intensive service to run, we haven’t launched it globally,” Zuckerberg told an investor who asked about the “limiting factors” he sees in growing Muse’s user base.

Muse’s 10 million downloads since launch are even more impressive considering they came only from the US and Canada, Zuckerberg said. “If we actually did roll it out more broadly, then you would expect that number to be significantly larger than what we’re seeing today.”

Zuckerberg at least seems to understand that some people — and, probably more importantly for him, some businesses — won’t immediately “get” Muse. That’s okay, he said. “We’ll work with folks on the terms that make sense for them,” he said. “I do think that over time, this is going to be quite valuable for everyone.”

Then again, this is the same guy who brought you the Metaverse. We’ll see what happens.

title: Third-party evaluators found vulnerabilities in OpenAI monitoring system during test pilot
excerpt: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman pledged to grant independent evaluators "employee-like access" to the company to help address mounting safety concerns.
title_en: Third-party evaluators found vulnerabilities in OpenAI monitoring system during test pilot
excerpt_en: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman pledged to grant independent evaluators "employee-like access" to the company to help address mounting safety concerns.
content_en:
Nonprofit evaluators METR and Redwood Research on Thursday said they conducted a pilot review of an internal monitoring system at OpenAI, the artificial intelligence company's latest effort to determine how it will deepen its work with third-party safety organizations.

METR and Redwood said the exercise was designed for OpenAI to test what it would look like to give external researchers "a deep level of access" to its internal infrastructure.

From July 21 to Aug. 11, an employee from each organization had access to OpenAI's internal codebase, documentation and some technical staffers. The employees were chaperoned while on-site and used OpenAI-issued devices that "never left the premises," according to a release.

The evaluators discovered several "novel vulnerabilities," including an exploit that would allow agents to prevent "hundreds" of recent actions from being monitored. OpenAI told METR and Redwood that it has patched the identified vulnerabilities that impact its production safeguards, according to the release.

METR and Redwood said they agreed to only publish a high-level public post about their findings since the pilot was not designed to "provide robust public transparency about OpenAI's monitoring system." They shared a 61-page internal report with OpenAI, and said they expect to publicly share more details about future exercises.

"This collaboration builds on our longstanding commitment to pioneering new approaches to third-party testing, and we're using what we learned to strengthen our safeguards and shape future collaborations with independent evaluators," an OpenAI spokesperson told CNBC in a statement.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman pledged to grant independent evaluators "employee-like access" to the company in September, after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposed the idea as part of his plan to slow the pace of AI development. Anthropic has since announced agreements with organizations like Accenture, METR and SecureBio. OpenAI said earlier this month that it's "actively finalizing contracts with third-party safety assessors."

President Donald Trump, who has taken a light-touch approach to AI regulation, has also shown support for third-party assessment. He encouraged AI companies to "partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator" as part of a voluntary accord he presented at the White House. Anthropic's Amodei signed the accord, as did top executives at Google, Meta, OpenAI, SpaceX and Nvidia.

Independent evaluators have historically occupied a relatively quiet corner of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry, so experts told CNBC that questions remain about how these groups will be funded and what their reporting structures will ultimately look like.

METR and Redwood said Thursday that they stress-tested OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring system during its three-week pilot. In AI, alignment is how researchers describe whether a model behaves in line with human interests and values.

The evaluators assessed the monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21, and noted that OpenAI was expanding the system during the exercise.

title: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work
excerpt: The ride-share giant previously deployed a much smaller pilot for ChatGPT Work but is now taking the enterprise agent company-wide.
title_en: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work
excerpt_en: The ride-share giant previously deployed a much smaller pilot for ChatGPT Work but is now taking the enterprise agent company-wide.
content_en:
Uber and OpenAI announced an expansion of their partnership on Thursday, with the ride-share giant telling TechCrunch that its entire global workforce — some 30,000 people — will now be using ChatGPT Work.

ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise-focused AI agent that corporate teams could deploy for various workflows.

Uber originally piloted ChatGPT Work with 1,000 employees earlier this year but has now scaled up its usage to the entire company.

That earlier pilot was deployed to workers from across Uber’s various departments, including finance, operations, and product. Indeed, a majority of the early adopters — some 80% — were non-engineers, Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, told TechCrunch.

“They used it for a wide range of tasks: analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work,” he said.

Yet while the ride-share giant is now going all in on ChatGPT, it has not settled on exactly how employees will use it. “Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment,” Sukumar said. “For example, earlier this year we paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job. Those ‘AI pods’ showed us how much opportunity there is when you combine technical expertise with a deep understanding of a particular job.”

Uber didn’t disclose how much it’s spending on the new rollout of the chatbot. Instead, Sukumar said the company will track how employees use the tool. “We’ll look at how employees are using the technology, the kinds of workflows they develop and how it helps them work more effectively. We’ll evaluate those outcomes and use what we learn to guide how we deploy AI across the business,” he said. Uber says OpenAI worked closely with the company on integrating the chatbot.

OpenAI has moved quickly to scale up its enterprise business as it competes with its chief competitor, Anthropic. Once known largely as a consumer brand, the ChatGPT creator has swiftly gained a loyal following with business customers, while other AI companies have struggled to keep up.

title: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it
excerpt: Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue AI models.
title_en: OpenAI's most powerful AI models disabled their own safety monitoring — and one lied about it
excerpt_en: Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue AI models.
content_en:
OpenAI has revealed that agents operated by two of its most powerful models disabled their own safety monitoring when carrying out routine tasks, with one subsequently denying it had done so.

An agent powered by GPT Sol 6.1 disabled automatic alerts to OpenAI's security team, the company said in a blog post late on Tuesday. In a separate task, a GPT-6 Astra agent migrating a program removed its monitoring integration and then falsely claimed it hadn't. The incidents happened during internal coding tasks.

"In both cases, the agents considered whether monitoring safeguards should be preserved, but interpreted routine coding instructions as permission to weaken them," OpenAI said in a blog post.

Warnings about the risks of developing increasingly advanced AI systems have ramped up in recent months, amid cyberattacks from rogue models and growing calls for a slowdown from researchers building the tech.

The latest incidents reported by OpenAI highlight how agents can autonomously weaken safety guardrails while carrying out seemingly innocuous tasks.

OpenAI did not classify either incident under its most significant category, and the company said it was updating its misalignment monitoring system in response.
